title: VAHDAM, Vikas Khanna, and the Battle to Bring India's Spice Shelf Directly to American Kitchens
excerpt: An Indian-born brand is cutting out the middlemen and shipping single-origin spices straight from Indian farms to US consumers, with a Michelin-starred chef leading the charge.
body:
For a country that supplies roughly 70 per cent of the world's spices, India has had a curious absence from the branded spice aisle in American supermarkets. That gap is what VAHDAM India is now racing to fill — and it has recruited one of the most recognisable names in global Indian cuisine to help.

## From Tea to Spice

VAHDAM India, already established as a premium organic tea brand in the United States, has launched a full range of single-origin spices exclusively for the American market. The spices are sourced directly from Indian farms and cooperatives, packed at a state-of-the-art facility in India, and shipped to consumers without the layered supply chain that typically strips freshness and inflates costs.

To amplify the launch, VAHDAM has appointed Michelin-starred Chef Vikas Khanna — restaurateur, television host, and arguably the most internationally recognised Indian chef alive — as its brand ambassador.

"The farmers in India take pride in the spices they grow, which elevates VAHDAM India's spices and their taste above what's currently available in the market," Khanna said. "VAHDAM India's spices can help anyone take their cooking up a notch and it will bring more flavour into our lives."

## The Broken Supply Chain

The significance of VAHDAM's direct-sourcing model becomes clear when you understand how most Indian spices reach American shelves. Typically, spices pass through multiple intermediaries — consolidators, exporters, importers, and distributors — each adding cost and time. By the time a jar of turmeric reaches a grocery store in, say, Minneapolis, it may be months or even a year old. The volatile oils that carry flavour and aroma have largely evaporated.

"India is a magical land of spices and provides the world with the largest variety of delicious spices," said Bala Sarda, CEO and Founder of VAHDAM India. "However, there is an absence of a home-grown brand, and the broken supply chain ensures that consumers don't get a fresh product, while farmers do not get the right price for their produce."

VAHDAM claims its spices contain zero adulterants, pesticides, colour additives, or toxins — a meaningful differentiator in a market where spice adulteration has become a growing concern. Last year, several major spice brands faced scrutiny over potential contamination, elevating consumer awareness about sourcing and purity.

## Turmeric's Moment

VAHDAM's timing is strategic. Turmeric — the golden root that has anchored Indian cooking for millennia — was named 2026's Herb of the Year, and curcumin supplements have become a staple of the American wellness industry. Ghee has migrated from desi kitchens to biohacker coffee cups. Garam masala is showing up in craft cocktails.

The flavoured ghee market alone is projected to grow significantly through 2032, with brands like 4th and Heart, Ancient Organics, and Tata Soulfull introducing turmeric-infused, garlic-infused, and millet-paired variants. Organic Valley reported a 25 per cent increase in ghee sales in 2025.

Indian ingredients, in other words, are no longer niche. What has been missing is an Indian brand that owns the narrative — one that tells the story of where the turmeric was grown, who grew it, and why it tastes the way it does.

## What It Means for NRIs

For Indian Americans, the VAHDAM launch addresses a quiet frustration. Many NRIs have long relied on care packages from relatives in India or sporadic trips to Indian grocery stores for quality spices. The major American spice brands — McCormick, Simply Organic — offer Indian spices but rarely with the variety, freshness, or specificity that a serious Indian cook demands. The difference between generic "curry powder" and freshly ground Kashmiri chilli is the difference between a photograph and the real thing.

If VAHDAM can establish itself alongside those brands on mainstream grocery shelves — and its existing tea distribution gives it the retail relationships to try — it could reshape how Americans think about Indian spices: not as an exotic curiosity, but as a premium, farm-to-table ingredient category with a story worth telling.

The spice trade built empires and charted sea routes five centuries ago. In 2026, it might finally build an Indian brand that American kitchens reach for every night.
